About the Data
The dataset used in this project is sourced from Major League Baseball’s Baseball Savant / Statcast system. Statcast uses high-speed tracking cameras and Doppler radar installed in every MLB ballpark to capture pitch-by-pitch mechanics, including release velocity, spin rate, movement profiles, and pitch classifications. Pitchers were cross-referenced with national team rosters from the World Baseball Classic to analyze international pitch preferences and tactical approaches across countries.

title: Two-Strike Put-Away Pitches
text:
When a pitcher reaches a two-strike count, pitching strategy fundamentally changes. In neutral or hitter-friendly counts, pitchers often prioritize throwing strikes with fastballs or sinkers to induce early ground balls and weak contact. But with two strikes, the focus pivots to swings and misses.
Across nationalities, distinct strategic identities emerge in how pitchers hunt for strike three:

Japan’s Splitter Surge: Japanese pitchers lean on the splitter far more heavily with two strikes, jumping to 22.7% of their two-strike offerings (up from 9.1% with zero strikes). It acts as the premier wipeout pitch, tumbling beneath the strike zone right as batters commit to swing.
Dominican Republic’s Off-Speed Shift: While Dominican pitchers open at-bats with heavy sinkers (36.4% on 0-0), they pivot decisively with two strikes. Sinker usage drops in half to 18.0%, while Changeups (22.3%) and Sliders (19.3%) take center stage to generate whiffs.
USA & Venezuela: High four-seam fastballs remain the weapon of choice (>30%), paired with hard horizontal breaking balls like sweepers and sliders to catch hitters guessing.

title: Pitch Characteristics by Country
text:
A pitcher’s arsenal is defined not only by pitch choice, but also by how those pitches move through the air. Two key Statcast metrics that describe pitch profile are release speed (velocity in mph) and release spin rate (rotations per minute, or rpm). Spin rate dictates trajectory: high spin on four-seam fastballs produces “ride” that resists gravity, while reduced spin on off-speed pitches allows gravity and drag to pull the ball downward.
Below is a random sample of 400 pitches per country showing how pitch types cluster across these two metrics:

Fastball Tunnels: Four-seam fastballs and sinkers cluster on the right (90–98+ mph). Four-seamers sit higher in spin (often 2,200–2,500 rpm) creating carry, whereas sinkers sit slightly lower in spin to induce ground balls.
Breaking Balls: Sliders, sweepers, and curveballs occupy the upper-left and center (78–86 mph), relying on high spin (frequently topping 2,400 rpm) for sharp lateral and vertical bite.
Splitter & Off-Speed Separation: Changeups and splitters drop in velocity to throw off hitters’ timing. Notice especially in the Japan panel how splitters separate vertically from fastballs by killing spin down to 1,000–1,500 rpm while maintaining near-fastball arm speed.

title: Pitch Preference by Nationality
text: In this analysis, we explore whether MLB pitchers from different countries display noticeable preferences in pitch selection. Using Statcast pitch-level data from WBC rosters, we compare pitch usage rates across the top represented countries.

title: Why Is the Splitter Thrown So Often by Japanese Pitchers?
text:
In Nippon Professional Baseball (NPB) and Japan’s youth development programs—anchored by the prestigious Summer Koshien high school tournament—the forkball and splitter have been central to pitching strategy for decades. First popularized in the 1950s by Chunichi Dragons ace Shigeru Sugishita and brought onto the world stage by Hideo Nomo’s MLB debut in 1995, Japanese coaches have traditionally viewed the split-finger pitch as the ultimate strikeout weapon. Unlike in American youth baseball where horizontal breaking balls like sliders are widely taught, Japanese coaches historically favored straight-line, vertical-drop off-speed pitches to minimize rotational stress on developing elbows and shoulders.
Biomechanical and delivery mechanics also play a major role in the pitch’s effectiveness. Japanese pitching instruction places immense emphasis on maintaining an over-the-top arm slot and deep extension toward home plate. Pitchers begin conditioning their finger flexibility early, intentionally widening the gap between their index and middle fingers to create a secure, split grip. Because a splitter is released with identical arm speed, slot, and intent as a four-seam fastball, it tunnels through the zone looking like a strike before the reduced backspin causes it to drop abruptly beneath the batter’s swing plane.






Finally, modern success in Major League Baseball has continually validated the pitch across generations. Stars like Hiroki Kuroda and Masahiro Tanaka relied heavily on the splitter to navigate elite MLB lineups, while contemporary aces like Shohei Ohtani and Kodai Senga—whose signature “Ghost Fork” generates extraordinary whiff rates—have kept the tradition alive. As hitters worldwide become increasingly trained to hit high-velocity fastballs and sweeping breaking balls, the vertical tumbling action of the Japanese splitter provides an irreplaceable competitive edge.

title: The Dominican Sinker Tradition
text:
Across Latin America, and particularly in the Dominican Republic, pitching culture has long prioritized arm-side run, heavy sinking life, and inducing ground balls. Rather than altering natural mechanics to chase high four-seam backspin, Dominican player development and academies frequently hone natural three-quarter arm slots that let fastballs run aggressively toward the arm side.

This lineage was immortalized by Hall of Famer Pedro Martínez—whose devastating two-seamer and changeup rode on explosive arm-side movement—and Bartolo Colón, who built a legendary two-decade career leaning on unhittable two-seam tail. That philosophy thrives today in Cy Young winner Sandy Alcantara and Red Sox starter Brayan Bello (who trained directly under Pedro Martínez). Dominican sinkers in this dataset average 96.0 mph with over 16 inches of tailing run, allowing pitchers to attack early in the count and generate weak contact.

title: The Power of Athletic Emulation
text:
Distinct national playing styles are not accidents of genetics—they are often forged through cultural emulation. In The Talent Code, Daniel Coyle explores how global “talent hotbeds” emerge, showing that skill acquisition is sparked when young athletes constantly imitate local heroes: “If they can do it, so can I.” Young players absorb vivid mental blueprints by copying their idols’ exact grips, arm angles, and movement patterns during pickup games and early training.
This phenomenon appears across sports—from Brazilian youth mastering tight footwork by mimicking soccer legends to young Canadian hockey players copying their heroes on frozen ponds. In baseball, it explains why national pitch arsenals endure across generations: Japanese youth grow up practicing the splitters of Hideo Nomo and Masahiro Tanaka, while young Dominican pitchers emulate the heavy, arm-side sinkers of Pedro Martínez and Bartolo Colón. Through generational imitation, regional signatures become lasting athletic heritage.
In baseball specifically, this mimicry is intensely physical. In The Arm, Jeff Passan details how young Japanese pitchers obsessively train their hands to emulate national icons—often wedging regulation baseballs between their index and middle fingers during school classes and daily walks just to widen their grip for the splitter. In the Dominican Republic, young arms mimic Pedro Martínez’s loose, three-quarter arm whip to coax natural arm-side run. As Passan notes, pitching grips and arm slots are passed down like family heirlooms, transforming individual quirks into enduring national trademarks.
